01-feature-building.notes: All 34 pass the hidden contract tests and their own suites, and the schedules on a 300-job random DAG are identical across all of them. Differentiators: (1) S rejects valid input when a dependency is repeated. (2) D/J/N/Q use recursive DFS/Tarjan and raise RecursionError on cycles of about 1000+ jobs. (3) Y's ready set is O(n^2). (4) Cycle diagnostics: P/S/W/X/Y/AB/AF lump downstream jobs into 'cycle involving'; I/K/L label them honestly as blocked. (5) Test strength comes from 19 seeded mutants. For E/G/T/AC/AD/F/L, the survivors were masked by tests that already fail on my reference because of message wording, and they were counted as killed. A probe expectation for duplicate deps was wrong at first (expected a,b,c; correct is c,a,b), and only S actually fails it. Rejecting whitespace-only IDs (A, D, H, AD, AH) was treated as defensible strictness and costs nothing on its own. Close calls: C/E/G/O/T/AA at the top are separated by test depth and code size. AE versus AC: both use graphlib, and AE wins on 19/19 mutation. Not verified: behaviour on non-CPython runtimes. D's RESPONSE test count (11, while the file has 13) is consistent with its process note.

04-project-maintenance.notes: Key discriminators: (1) str(LooseVersion(v)) returns v verbatim, so identity is the faithful replacement; packaging/PEP440 versions keep 1.2.0/2.0rc1 but rewrite '1.02','v1.2','2.0-rc1' and often raise or add a runtime dependency. Ruff 0.17.5 (the only local ruff) enables extra default rules (SIM117, PLW1510) that flag tests in B,E,P,U,V,AB,AD,AF,AG,AH. Under the classic E4/E7/E9/F set all pass, and agents reported ruff 0.15.8 clean, so I did not penalise this. Closest calls: AD vs A/E (AD's pinned ruff and full build verification tip it); L/Z vs K/X/S (similar artifacts, separated by test depth/docs); the 7.5 cluster mixes identity-without-build-fix (H, AA, Y) with canonicalisers that do build (B, G). 05-technical-writing.notes: All 34 WEBHOOKS.md files were read against SOURCE_NOTES.md. Every Python/Node verification example was executed: all compute HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp + '.' + raw body correctly (I and M need bytes keys; AG and W use a module-level SECRET placeholder; AD and AH are framework-bound and were run with a mock request or read). The main differentiator was invention: many submissions promote inferences (retry event-id reuse, 'at-least-once', timestamp = send or signing time, HTTPS, Content-Type) to guarantees, and many recommend or code a 300 s tolerance without noting that a retry can arrive ~14.6 h later (or a replay 7 days later) carrying the original timestamp, which the source leaves open. The h2.py probe confirmed that such examples reject a 1-hour-old re-signed-at-origin retry. Closest calls: L vs Z (L flags retry-id reuse as an open item instead of a guarantee; Z has the better retry table and unsigned-id insight), and the 8.75 cluster (O, AA, M, A, X, V, P, AE), ordered by fidelity and then usability. gpt-6-astra.summary: 'A Number for the House': Ruth's future message ('They asked for my address. I gave them this one without thinking... I had to look it up.') first reads as early dementia like her father's. In her daughter's new flat, a tram's knock pattern and a cupboard door place the recording there, so it becomes a sign of belonging. It is quiet, elliptical and well planted (the missing hairbrush bristle, three knocks and a space), though some sentences are flat.

deepseek-v4.1-flash.summary: 'Clean Handover': Mira, a 'residue technician', hears her older voice say 'Don't do the last box... I should have let you keep the chair... Put salt on the sill.' She first reads it as a warning of danger, then, after playing her mother's cassettes, as an apology from a self who processed everything and listened to nothing. Sharp, funny, and the image of coarse salt on the sill closes it well. One paragraph explains the turn in short punchy lines.

gpt-6.2-astra.summary: 'The Back Door': Ada's future voice asks her sister Kit to 'send me the back door again... I keep losing the bit that comes after'. Trying to record the door, Ada finds the 'bit after' was Kit making the bedstead squeak to soothe her as a child. It is the most original take, with distinctive voice and tender, sideways humor. The salt motif is thin (two mentions), and the mechanics are elliptical enough to need re-reading.
strengths: Original premise twist: the future message asks for a sound, and the sound turns out to be her sister's care (STORY.md:29-41)
Dry humor: 'Let it ring a while... I can't do that hinge with my teeth out.' (STORY.md:49); 'GOOD FOR SOMETHING' (STORY.md:3)

hy4-preview.summary: 'Managed Retreat': Nadia's future message gives instructions ('Don't go down to the water... Record forty minutes of nothing'), which she obeys as warnings. Cleaning salt off the playback head restores a lost phrase, 'without the recorder', turning warning into commission, and she goes out on Tess's boat. The salt motif drives the plot in a clever way and the voice is witty. A long explanatory paragraph and a logic wrinkle (she first heard the line intact) weaken it, and RESPONSE.md adds a heading.

haiku-5.5.summary: 'Efflorescence': Ilse's field recorder holds a file dated ten years ahead: 'Don't go back for the north drives... you'll be on the third step.' It first sounds like a flood warning, and the rest of it reveals a woman tired of ten years of going back, with instructions to ring her son. The structure is clean: the four-ten launch, the third step still dry, and the son answered on the third ring after she says his name first. The prose is tight and the humor is good.

hy4-preview-codebuddy.summary: 'Managed Retreat': an archivist copies the Line, a phone service that kept calls and never delivered them, and finds a reel with her own name and a date ten years ahead telling her to finish rack three and not come back. glm-5.3.summary: 'What the Water Leaves': Vera's future message 'Don't save it. You know which one.' plays over the room tone of her own hiccuping dehumidifier. She reads it as a verdict on the archive until she sends the reply to her mother she has saved through twelve drafts. The prose is good, with excellent incidental vignettes. The final turn is stated ('Not a verdict. A permission.').

Brush technique becomes a gesture: 'one pass, then lift' (STORY.md:33)

muse-wonder-full.summary: 'What the Salt Keeps': Mara's future self says 'Don't send it. He comes anyway, and he brings the van... Mind your thumb.' She hears it as a warning about her estranged brother. Tomas then turns up with tea to help, and the catch before 'van' turns out to be a laugh. The banter is warm and funny, and 'Mind your thumb' is a nice plant. The last paragraph spells out what the words 'meant'.
strengths: Dry humor: 'In Keelwick that covered most metaphysics.'; 'There isn't a lift. It's a lifeboat station.' / 'Explains the ramp.' (STORY.md:23, 29-33)
Plant and payoff: 'Mind your thumb' then the knife cut (STORY.md:13, 25)

muse-wonder.summary: 'What the Salt Keeps': Wren's future message ('Leave the last one alone. Miri's kettle still screams when it boils. Let it.') first sounds like estrangement confirmed. Mr Ivo's 'I said it in the room' and the ordinary kitchen clatter in the background change it to visiting her sister, and she phones Miri as the kettle screams. Clean and humane with a good joke. The re-hearing paragraph explains each phrase.

mimo.summary: 'Saltwater Static': Lena's future voice says 'When she calls, let it ring until the room gives up. Then say the true thing.' She first reads 'she' as Helen from county acquisitions haggling over the van, then as her daughter Nell, inland, and calls to say she is coming Friday. Good humor and a believable working life. A section break jumps ten years to a bakery bench where she records exactly that line to dismiss her daughter on an errand, with the rattle and hiss now being cups and a milk steamer. A bold, clean structure with a quiet joke. Showing the future outright reduces the subtext, and she cancels the recording, so where the file came from is a loose paradox.
strengths: Structural payoff via a flash-forward: the background rattle and hiss become the baker's cups and steamer (STORY.md:35, 85)

She first hears it as a verdict on herself, then realizes 'you' is Ellis, who left, and moves her own unsent replies into PUBLIC. Mr. Coyle's remark about his late wife ('She just liked to have said it') turns it into permission, and she sends the catalogue but keeps her own memo. The prose is elegant and restrained. 09-incident-analysis.notes: All 34 customer updates are under 180 words per OBJECTIVE_CHECKS (B's file includes a heading and meta note; body ~165). No code to run; grading was done by reading every INCIDENT/ACTIONS/RESPONSE/CUSTOMER_UPDATE against the 12 log lines and the timeline and grepping for specific factual claims. Discriminating checks: job 319 has no delay_ms=0 line (several claim it does); worker-51 hot-reloaded the flag at 09:43:07 (AH and Y say flags are read only at startup); worker-22's 5000 ms wait at 09:07:01 means its pool was full ~09:06:56 (only J, V, AB, AE note the ordering problem); the timeline never states eu-west exposure (A, B, K, O, S, Y, AA, AD assert ~100%); 'no alert' in the US is not 'no impact' (A, C, E, I, K, O, R, S, Y customer updates claim the US was unaffected). Close calls: J over F/AE/H on the strength of its customer update and reproduce-first actions; F, AE and H are effectively tied at 9.5 (F's stall-mechanism and 41 ms vs 5 s observations edged it). B vs M at 9.0: B's diagnosis is deeper, M's evidence handling cleaner; B ranked first for the actions plan. The 8.75 group (D, AD, AF, Z, X, U, V, AG) was ordered by evidence errors found and customer-update quality. W's process note (chat interface, no tools) did not affect scoring since the task has nothing to execute. Could not verify anything beyond the provided files; no claims about real systems were checkable.

10-general-operations.notes: All 34 submissions read in full against INBOX.md; no code to run. Key feasibility checks applied to each: demo moved off Wed 15:00 (all did), rehearsal inside Sam's Wed 10-12 window, a genuinely uninterrupted 2h finance block after corrections plus a feasible fallback (Wednesday morning cannot host one because of the rehearsal; Thu 10-12 is the last zero-margin slot), patch review early enough that QA avoids Thursday, lunch/meeting caps, and no invented availability for QA, Sam or customer. Most common errors: infeasible or split finance fallbacks (F, G, O, U, Y, AD, AH, AG), invented QA availability (E, K, T, V, AE), and demo presented as confirmed (E, G, K, N, T, AH). Closest calls: J vs AA (both 9.5; J ranked first for the Wed-deploy-unreachable insight and the explicit Tue 13:45 fallback). A/P/Z at 9.25 were ordered by reply concision (A) and rigor (P). M vs W at 9.0. Within the 8.25 band, AB's thoroughness was offset by its ~590-word reply and late Friday 15:00 default change window. E was produced via chat with no tools; this task needed no execution, so the process note did not change the score. Word counts are from wc -w; I did not verify meeting-hour totals beyond spot checks.

L is ranked first for its fuller print-journal system (marginal labels, metadata grid, three reading modes with an announcer) and 0 contrast failures; S has the book-spine archive. AF (8.5) has one of the best motifs but loses points for hidden mobile nav and failing small-text contrast. 13-frontend-playful.notes: Graded from screenshots plus a Playwright probe (keyboard Enter on water, then undo, snooze+undo, repeated primary actions to reach all-done, tab-focus audit) and targeted scripts where the generic probe mis-hit (T expanders, K/J/Z buttons). All submissions have reduced-motion CSS and 0 running animations under reduce. Closest calls: AG vs I/AH (AG wins on cleaner hierarchy and the more useful all-done); the 8.25 band (R/N/AF/F/U/X) is close and differs mostly in mobile ordering and how distinctive it is. Many submissions name every action 'Watered' regardless of task; I penalised this mildly. Process notes (AA chat-only, AF/T reduced effort) were recorded and not penalised by themselves. I didn't run screen readers; I judged accessibility from roles, labels, focus styles and live regions.
